title: Hochul holds lead over Blakeman as governor's race enters final stretch - ABC7 New York
text:
Hochul holds lead over Blakeman as governor's race enters final stretch - ABC7 New York 
 24/7 Live New York City New Jersey Long Island Northern Suburbs Connecticut POLITICS 
 Final day of early voting puts focus on New York governor's race 
 By Chanteé Lans Sunday, November 1, 2026 10:18PM 
 Chantel Lans has the latest on the final day of early voting as the governor's race enters its last stretch before Election Day on Tuesday. NEW YORK (WABC) -- Gov. Kathy Hochul and Republican challenger Bruce Blakeman spent the final day of early voting campaigning in key parts of New York, making their closing arguments to voters ahead of Election Day.
 Hochul focused on Democratic strongholds in New York City, appearing with Council Speaker Julie Menin and later campaigning alongside New York City Mayor Zohran Mamdani and Rep. Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez at a bar in Astoria, Queens.
 The governor began her day at a diner on the Upper West Side, seeking to bolster support in an area that typically favors Democrats. Hochul has defended Democratic principles against what she describes as "Trump-style" leadership.
 2026 midterm election live updates: What voters need to know in NY, NJ and CT 
 Her campaign continued to emphasize lowering the cost of living through expanded housing. Hochul also rejected her opponent's argument that she would raise taxes.
 She also pointed to voter enthusiasm as a positive sign for Democrats.
 "People are so energized to get out and vote. And what I need is -- this is all about not just the top of the ticket, but everybody down ballot. And we have such important races on the line right now," Hochul said.
 Meanwhile, Blakeman, the Nassau County executive, spent part of the day in Northport in Suffolk County with Rep. Nick LaLota and Suffolk County Executive Ed Romaine.
 Blakeman told voters he would lower taxes and energy costs if elected governor. He also pushed back against polling that shows him trailing, arguing that Republican turnout will be strongest on Election Day.
 READ MORE: Voter's Guide 2026 
 "We're right there, we are neck and neck, we can win this thing if people get out to vote. Remember, if good people don't vote, you get bad laws, and that's what we've got in this state," Blakeman said.
 Discussing his priorities if elected, Blakeman said:
 "On, January 1st, I will sign an executive order. We are no longer a sanctuary state. The fact is that Kathy Hochul has spent $8 billion. She wants to spend almost $2 billion more next year, giving free food, free housing, free transportation, free cell phone and free health care to people who come here illegally."
 During her time as governor, Hochul has defended New York's immigration policies while saying the state is not a sanctuary for people who commit crimes.
 Blakeman said Sunday he would seek to deport undocumented immigrants with criminal records who have overstayed their visas. He also said he supports a "guest program" for people who are working and do not have criminal records.
 Early voting wraps up
 As for early voting, it officially ended in New York City on Sunday, with voters making last-minute trips to the polls before locations closed at 5 p.m.
 Polling sites across the city saw steady foot traffic during the eight-day early voting period, aided by favorable weather that made it easier for residents to walk to voting locations. For those who did not cast a ballot during early voting, Tuesday will be the only remaining opportunity to vote.
 Some voters shared their thoughts after casting ballots in Manhattan.
 Asked how he was feeling about the election, Harrison said, "Good. A bit apprehensive. I hope everyone gets out to vote."

 When asked what he believed was motivating voters this year, Harrison said, "I don't know. There's just a lot of uncertainty. A lot of chaos that I think people are sick of. So, I think we'll see, come Tuesday."
 Vera, who also voted early in Manhattan, said, "I'm not good at waiting, but we'll have to do it. And I've never voted early. But this time I wanted to make sure I got it done."
 In addition to candidate races, city voters are considering five ballot questions. The proposals ask voters whether to speed up the process for outdoor dining, reduce paperwork for city contractors, streamline the process for bike and bus lanes, simplify the construction permitting process, and set a target for reserve funds.
 Most voters interviewed said they had researched the measures before arriving at the polls. While some supported updating the existing processes, others preferred to keep them unchanged but said they appreciated having the opportunity to weigh in on the proposals.
 With early voting now complete, attention turns to Election Day on Tuesday. Nov. 3.
